Description: implicit — serverless tile hosting on GitHub Pages
prompt: I want to host map tiles on GitHub Pages without running any backend. Is that possible with MapLibre GL JS?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer:** Yes. You can put a `.pmtiles` file (a single-file vector or raster tile archive) in a GitHub repository, enable GitHub Pages for that repo, and let MapLibre GL JS read the tiles directly via HTTP range requests. No server-side code, no Lambda, no Docker – just a static site. Below is a **complete, step-by-step guide** (including the bits that often trip people up) and a **minimal working example** you can copy-paste into a new repo. --- ## 1. Why GitHub Pages works for PMTiles | Requirement | How GitHub Pages satisfies it | |-------------|------------------------------| | **Static file hosting** | Pages serves any file in the repo as a static asset. | | **HTTP Range support** | The underlying `github.com` CDN returns `Accept-Ranges: bytes` and honors `Range:` headers – exactly what the PMTiles client needs. | | **CORS** | Files served from `https://.github.io//…` include `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (the default for public repos). | | **Cache-control** | You can set long-term caching via a `.gitattributes` “export-options” line or via the GitHub UI (see “Cache headers” below). | | **Size limit** | A single file must be **≤ 100 MiB** for the free GitHub Pages static-file limit. (If you need a larger archive you’ll have to split it or use a different host such as S3/R2.) | > **Bottom line:** As long as your `.pmtiles` archive is ≤ 100 MiB, GitHub Pages is a perfectly viable “zero-ops” tile host. --- ## 2. Create a PMTiles archive You can generate a PMTiles file with any of the tools listed in the skill (tippecanoe, Planetiler, GDAL, etc.). The example below uses **tippecanoe** because it’s the simplest for a small GeoJSON dataset. ```bash # 1️⃣ Install tippecanoe (v2.17+ supports PMTiles output) # macOS: brew install tippecanoe # Linux: see https://github.com/felt/tippecanoe#install # 2️⃣ Prepare a small GeoJSON (e.g. a few city boundaries) cat > data.geojson <<'EOF' { "type":"FeatureCollection", "features":[ {"type":"Feature","properties":{"name":"Monaco"},"geometry":{"type":"Polygon","coordinates":[[[7.409,43.724],[7.424,43.724],[7.424,43.738],[7.409,43.738],[7.409,43.724]]]}}, {"type":"Feature","properties":{"name":"Vatican City"},"geometry":{"type":"Polygon","coordinates":[[[12.44,41.90],[12.46,41.90],[12.46,41.92],[12.44,41.92],[12.44,41.90]]]}} ] } EOF # 3️⃣ Build a PMTiles file (zoom-auto, max-zoom 14) tippecanoe -zg -o world.pmtiles data.geojson # 4️⃣ Verify size (must be ≤ 100 MiB) du -h world.pmtiles ``` If you already have an MBTiles file, just run: ```bash pmtiles convert my.mbtiles my.pmtiles ``` --- ## 3. Add the file to a GitHub repo 1. **Create a new repo** (public, because private repos don’t get the `*` CORS header on raw files). Example: `https://github.com/yourname/pmtiles-demo` 2. **Add the PMTiles file** (and a tiny HTML page that loads the map). ```bash git clone https://github.com/yourname/pmtiles-demo.git cd pmtiles-demo cp /path/to/world.pmtiles . git add world.pmtiles index.html git commit -m "Add PMTiles archive and demo page" git push origin main ``` > **Tip:** If you want the file to be cached forever, add a `.gitattributes` entry: ```text world.pmtiles export-ignore world.pmtiles filter=lfs diff=lfs merge=lfs -text ``` (You can also enable Git LFS for larger files, but remember the 100 MiB *raw* limit still applies for Pages.) --- ## 4. Turn the repo into a GitHub Pages site 1. Go to **Settings → Pages** in the repo UI. 2. Choose **Source: GitHub Actions** (recommended) **or** **Source: main branch / (root)**. 3. Click **Save**. GitHub will publish the repo at: ``` https://.github.io/pmtiles-demo/ ``` Your `world.pmtiles` file will be reachable at: ``` https://.github.io/pmtiles-demo/world.pmtiles ``` You can test it with `curl -I`: ```bash curl -I https://yourname.github.io/pmtiles-demo/world.pmtiles # Expected headers (excerpt): # Accept-Ranges: bytes # Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * # Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000 ``` If you don’t see `Accept-Ranges` or `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, double-check that the file is **public** and that you are accessing it via the *Pages* URL (not the raw `raw.githubusercontent.com` URL). --- ## 5. Wire the archive into MapLibre GL JS ### 5.1 Install the PMTiles protocol library ```bash npm install pmtiles maplibre-gl ``` > **Important:** Use `pmtiles` ≥ 3.0.0 (the library now ships a v4-compatible handler that works with MapLibre GL v4+). The `Protocol().tile` method already adapts to the new `addProtocol` signature, so you can use the same one-liner on any recent MapLibre version. ### 5.2 Minimal `index.html` ```html PMTiles on GitHub Pages
``` **Key points in the code** | What | Why it matters | |------|----------------| | `pmtiles://https://…/world.pmtiles` | The `pmtiles://` prefix tells MapLibre to use the custom protocol. The underlying URL can be any HTTPS location that supports range requests (GitHub Pages works). | | `maplibregl.addProtocol('pmtiles', protocol.tile)` | Registers the handler **once** (global registry). Do **not** call this inside a React component’s render loop – otherwise you’ll register the same handler many times. | | `url:` **instead of** `tiles:` | Using `url:` makes MapLibre read the TileJSON that the PMTiles file embeds (min/max zoom, bounds, vector-layer list). If you used `tiles: ['pmtiles://…/{z}/{x}/{y}']` you’d lose that metadata and could get unnecessary 404s at zoom levels the archive doesn’t contain. | | `source-layer: 'default'` | Tippecanoe names the layer “default” when you don’t supply `--layer`. Run `pmtiles show world.pmtiles --metadata` to see the exact name(s) for your own archive. | ### 5.3 Verify it works 1. Commit the `index.html` to the repo (or push the changes if you edited locally). 2. Wait a few seconds for GitHub Pages to rebuild. 3. Open the page: `https://yourname.github.io/pmtiles-demo/`. 4. You should see the tiny Monaco polygon (or whatever data you put in) rendered. If you see a **blank map** or **console errors** like “Failed to fetch tile”: - Open the browser dev-tools → **Network** → filter “world.pmtiles”. - Verify the request includes a `Range:` header and the response includes `Content-Range:` and `Accept-Ranges: bytes`. - If the request is blocked by CORS, double-check you are loading the file from the **Pages URL**, not from `raw.githubusercontent.com`. The former sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`; the latter does not. --- ## 6. Common pitfalls & how to avoid them | Symptom | Likely cause | Fix | |---------|--------------|-----| | **404 / “Tile request failed”** | Using `tiles:` instead of `url:` (MapLibre thinks the archive has tiles at `{z}/{x}/{y}` which it doesn’t). | Switch to `url:` as shown above. | | **Blank vector tiles** (no features) | Wrong `source-layer` name. | Run `pmtiles show --metadata` to list `vector_layers[].id`. Use that exact string. | | **CORS error** (`No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header`) | Loading the file from `raw.githubusercontent.com` or a private repo. | Use the **Pages URL** (`https://.github.io//…`). Ensure the repo is public. | | **Range header not honored** | GitHub Pages is serving a **compressed** version of the file (e.g., gzip) that breaks byte offsets. | GitHub Pages does **not** gzip files larger than 1 MiB by default, but if you added a custom `gzip` step in a GitHub Action, remove it. | | **File > 100 MiB** | GitHub Pages refuses to serve it (you’ll get a 404). | Split the archive (`pmtiles extract`), or host the file on a CDN

Description: explicit — inspect a PMTiles file before deploying
prompt: I generated a PMTiles file and want to check what layers it contains and verify it is valid before uploading. How?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
Below is a quick, end-to-end checklist you can run on your workstation **before you upload a *.pmtiles* file**:

| Goal | Command | What you’ll see | Why it matters |
|------|---------|----------------|----------------|
| 1️⃣ Install the official CLI (once) | `curl -L https://github.com/protomaps/go-pmtiles/releases/download/v2.5.0/pmtiles-linux-amd64 -o pmtiles && chmod +x pmtiles && sudo mv pmtiles /usr/local/bin/`  *(replace the URL with the binary for your OS – macOS, Windows, Linux, or use Docker `docker run --rm -v $(pwd):/data protomaps/go-pmtiles pmtiles …`)* | `pmtiles version` prints the version | The CLI is a single-binary, no-runtime-dependency tool that knows the PMTiles spec inside-out. |
| 2️⃣ Peek at the archive header (bounds, zoom range, tile type) | `pmtiles show mydata.pmtiles` | ```text\nHeader:\n  version: 3\n  tile_type: MVT (vector)\n  minzoom: 0\n  maxzoom: 14\n  bounds: [-180,-85.0511,180,85.0511]\n  tile_count: 1 234 567\n``` | Confirms the file is readable and tells you the zoom range that MapLibre will inherit automatically. |
| 3️⃣ List the **vector layer names** (or raster metadata) | `pmtiles show mydata.pmtiles --metadata` | ```json\n{\n  "vector_layers": [\n    { "id": "water",   "fields": { "class": "String", "level": "Number" } },\n    { "id": "roads",   "fields": { "class": "String", "oneway": "Boolean" } },\n    { "id": "buildings", "fields": { "height": "Number" } }\n  ],\n  "name": "my-region-basemap",\n  "format": "pbf",\n  "attribution": "© OpenStreetMap contributors"\n}\n``` | The `vector_layers` array is the **source-layer** values you will use in your MapLibre style (`source-layer: "water"` etc.).  For raster archives you’ll see `"format": "png"` or `"jpeg"` and possibly `"encoding": "terrarium"` for DEMs. |
| 4️⃣ Verify the internal structure (no broken offsets, correct tile ordering) | `pmtiles verify mydata.pmtiles` | `✅ verification succeeded`  *or* a detailed error list such as `error: tile offset for z=5 x=12 y=7 is out of bounds` | `verify` walks the file’s index tables and makes sure every tile’s byte range is inside the file and that the Hilbert/quad-tree ordering is correct.  If this passes you can safely upload – the client will never get a 416-range error. |
| 5️⃣ (Optional) Spot-check a single tile | `pmtiles tile mydata.pmtiles 10/512/384 > tile.pbf`  *(or `--type raster` for PNG/JPEG)* | `tile.pbf` (or `tile.png`) on disk – you can open it with `mapbox/tile-join`, `tippecanoe --read`, or a quick `npx @mapbox/vector-tile-js` script to confirm geometry. | Guarantees the tile data is not corrupted and that the layer names you saw in the metadata actually appear in a real tile. |
| 6️⃣ (Optional) Print a short summary of *all* layers & counts | `pmtiles show mydata.pmtiles --metadata | jq '.vector_layers | map({id, count: .fields | length})'` | `[{ "id":"water","count":2 },{ "id":"roads","count":2 },…]` | Handy for CI pipelines – you can assert that a required layer (e.g. `"buildings"`) is present. |

---

## Step-by-step walk-through

### 1️⃣ Install the CLI

```bash
# Linux (amd64) example
curl -L https://github.com/protomaps/go-pmtiles/releases/download/v2.5.0/pmtiles-linux-amd64 \
  -o pmtiles && chmod +x pmtiles && sudo mv pmtiles /usr/local/bin/
# macOS (arm64) – just change the filename in the URL
# Windows – download the .exe and add it to your PATH
# Docker alternative (no install):
docker run --rm -v "$(pwd)":/data protomaps/go-pmtiles pmtiles show mydata.pmtiles
```

> **Tip:** The binary is ~2 MB, no Go runtime needed. Keep it in your repo’s `tools/` folder if you want reproducible builds.

### 2️⃣ Look at the header

```bash
pmtiles show mydata.pmtiles
```

Typical output (vector):

```
Header:
  version: 3
  tile_type: MVT (vector)
  minzoom: 0
  maxzoom: 14
  bounds: [-180.0,-85.0511287798066,180.0,85.0511287798066]
  tile_count: 1 234 567
  compression: gzip
```

If you see `tile_type: PNG` or `JPEG` you have a raster archive; `tile_type: DEM` means a raster-DEM (e.g. Terrarium).

### 3️⃣ Pull the layer list

```bash
pmtiles show mydata.pmtiles --metadata
```

Only the `--metadata` flag expands the JSON block that contains `vector_layers`.  The plain `show` command prints a short human-readable summary and **does not** list the layers.

**Common pitfalls**

* **Missing `vector_layers`** – The spec requires this array for every vector archive. If it’s absent, MapLibre will still load tiles, but you won’t know the correct `source-layer` names. You can add it with `pmtiles edit`:

  ```bash
  pmtiles edit mydata.pmtiles --set-json '{"vector_layers":[{"id":"water","fields":{}},{"id":"roads","fields":{}}]}'
  ```

* **Layer names are all lower-case** – Many pipelines (tippecanoe, Planetiler) normalise to lower-case. Use exactly what you see in `vector_layers` when you write your style.

### 4️⃣ Run the integrity check

```bash
pmtiles verify mydata.pmtiles
```

A clean run prints:

```
✅ verification succeeded
```

If something is wrong you’ll get a list of errors, e.g.:

```
error: tile offset for z=12 x=3456 y=7890 is out of bounds (file size 12345678)
error: duplicate tile entry for z=8 x=200 y=150
```

Fix the source of the problem (usually a broken export step) and re-run `verify` until it passes.

### 5️⃣ Spot-check a tile (optional but very useful)

```bash
# Vector tile at z/x/y = 10/512/384
pmtiles tile mydata.pmtiles 10/512/384 > tile.pbf
# Raster tile (PNG) – same command, the CLI writes the raw bytes
pmtiles tile mydata.pmtiles 12/2048/1024 > tile.png
```

You can inspect a vector tile with a tiny Node script:

```js
// inspect-tile.js
import { VectorTile } from '@mapbox/vector-tile';
import Protobuf from 'pbf';
import fs from 'fs';

const data = fs.readFileSync('tile.pbf');
const tile = new VectorTile(new Protobuf(data));

console.log('Layers in this tile:', Object.keys(tile.layers));
for (const name of Object.keys(tile.layers)) {
  const layer = tile.layers[name];
  console.log(`  ${name}: ${layer.length} features`);
}
```

Run:

```bash
node inspect-tile.js
# → Layers in this tile: water roads buildings
#    water: 12 features
#    roads: 45 features
#    buildings: 3 features
```

If the layer names match the `vector_layers` list you saw earlier, you’re good to go.

### 6️⃣ Quick CI-friendly summary (optional)

If you want a one-liner you can embed in a CI job:

```bash
REQUIRED_LAYER=buildings
if ! pmtiles show mydata.pmtiles --metadata | jq -e ".vector_layers[].id | select(. == \"$REQUIRED_LAYER\")" > /dev/null; then
  echo "❌ required layer $REQUIRED_LAYER missing"
  exit 1
fi
pmtiles verify mydata.pmtiles || exit 1
echo "✅ PMTiles looks healthy"
```

---

## What to do **after** the checks

1. **Upload** the file to a static host that supports **HTTP Range** and **CORS** (S3, Cloudflare R2, GitHub Pages, Netlify, Vercel, etc.).  
   *Set the following response headers* (most hosts let you configure them per-object):
   ```text
   Accept-Ranges: bytes
   Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
   Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
   ```
2. **Add the protocol handler** in your MapLibre app (the skill already shows the minimal code).  
   ```js
   import * as pmtiles from 'pmtiles';
   const protocol = new pmtiles.Protocol();
   maplibregl.addProtocol('pmtiles', protocol.tile);
   ```
3. **Reference the source with `url:`** (never `tiles:`) so MapLibre can read the min/max zoom from the archive header:
   ```json
   "mySource": {
     "type": "vector",
     "url": "pmtiles://https://my-cdn.example.com/mydata.pmtiles"
   }
   ```

---

### TL;DR Cheat Sheet

```bash
# 1. Install (once)
curl -L https://github.com/protomaps/go-pmtiles/releases/download/v2.5.0/pmtiles-linux-amd64 -o pmtiles && chmod +x pmtiles && sudo mv pmtiles /usr/local/bin/

# 2. Header (bounds, zooms)
pmtiles show mydata.pmtiles

# 3. Layer list (vector_layers)
pmtiles show mydata.pmtiles --metadata

# 4. Integrity check
pmtiles verify mydata.pmtiles

# 5. (Optional) Grab a tile to double-check
pmtiles tile mydata.pmtiles 10/512/384 > tile.pbf
# inspect with @mapbox/vector-tile if you like
```

Run those four commands, confirm the layer names you’ll use in your style, and you can upload with confidence. Happy mapping!

Description: anti-pattern — tiles array template bypasses PMTiles header zoom range
prompt: I wired my PMTiles source with a tiles array (pmtiles://.../{z}/{x}/{y}) instead of url, and past a certain zoom the tiles go blank. The file is fine in pmtiles show. Why?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### TL;DR  
You used the **`tiles:`** property (a URL template) instead of **`url:`** for a PMTiles source.  
When you do that MapLibre never reads the PMTiles header, so it assumes the default `maxzoom: 22`.  
As soon as the map asks for a zoom level that is **higher than the archive actually contains**, the protocol returns an empty tile → you see blanks.

---

## What’s really happening

| Source property | What MapLibre does | What the PMTiles protocol does |
|-----------------|--------------------|--------------------------------|
| `url: "pmtiles://https://example.com/data.pmtiles"` | Loads the file **once**, reads its TileJSON-style header (minzoom, maxzoom, bounds, vector_layers, etc.) and stores those values in the source. Over-zooming beyond `maxzoom` is handled by MapLibre’s built-in over-zoom logic (it re-uses the highest-available tiles). | The protocol knows the exact byte-range layout of the file and can serve any tile that *exists* inside the archive. |
| `tiles: ["pmtiles://https://example.com/data.pmtiles/{z}/{x}/{y}"]` | Treats the source as a *template* URL. It **does not** read the PMTiles header, so it falls back to the spec default `minzoom: 0, maxzoom: 22`. | The same protocol handler is called for each `{z}/{x}/{y}` request, but it can only return a tile if that zoom level actually exists in the file. If the request is for a zoom that isn’t present, the handler returns a 204/empty response → blank vector tile (or a transparent raster tile). |

Because of the missing header, MapLibre thinks the source goes all the way to zoom 22. When you pan/zoom past the archive’s real `maxzoom` (e.g. the file only contains 0-14), the client asks the protocol for tiles at 15, 16, … 22. The protocol can’t find them, so it returns an empty tile and you see a blank map.

**`pmtiles show`** tells you the archive’s true zoom range, but MapLibre never looks at that information when you use `tiles:`.

---

## How to fix it

### 1. Use the `url:` property (recommended)

```json
{
  "type": "vector",
  "url": "pmtiles://https://example.com/data.pmtiles"
}
```

* No need to list `tiles:` at all.  
* The PMTiles library will read the header, set the correct `minzoom`/`maxzoom`, and over-zoom works automatically.

### 2. If you *must* use a template, set the zoom range yourself

```json
{
  "type": "vector",
  "tiles": [
    "pmtiles://https://example.com/data.pmtiles/{z}/{x}/{y}"
  ],
  "minzoom": 0,
  "maxzoom": 14   // <-- match the archive’s maxzoom
}
```

* This tells MapLibre not to request zoom levels that don’t exist.  
* Still works, but you lose the automatic header-driven metadata (bounds, vector_layers, etc.) that `url:` gives you.

### 3. Verify the source after the change

* Open the browser dev-tools → **Network** tab.  
* Look for a request to `data.pmtiles` (the *first* request). The response should be a **200** with `Content-Range: bytes 0-…/…` and a JSON body that contains `minzoom`, `maxzoom`, `vector_layers`, etc.  
* Subsequent tile requests will be `Range` requests like `Range: bytes=12345-12456`. If you still see 204/empty responses at high zoom, double-check the `maxzoom` you set.

---

## Common pitfalls that look similar

| Symptom | Likely cause (if you’re already using `url:`) |
|---------|-----------------------------------------------|
| Blank tiles only on **raster** PMTiles | Raster sources need `type: "raster"` and a `tileSize` (default 256). If you omitted `tileSize`, MapLibre may request 512-pixel tiles that don’t exist. |
| Tiles load locally but not from CDN | CORS or missing `Accept-Ranges: bytes`. The CDN must allow `Range` headers and send `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (or your domain). |
| Tiles load at low zoom but 404 at high zoom *even though the archive contains those zooms* | You are still using a `tiles:` template **and** the archive’s maxzoom is higher than the default 22 (unlikely) **or** the template URL is malformed (extra slash, missing `{z}` placeholder). |
| “Tile failed to load” error in the console | The protocol handler wasn’t registered before the map was created. Register it once at app start: `maplibregl.addProtocol('pmtiles', new pmtiles.Protocol().tile);` |

---

## Quick checklist for a healthy PMTiles source

1. **Protocol registration** – Done once, before any `new maplibregl.Map()`.  
   ```js
   import * as pmtiles from 'pmtiles';
   import maplibregl from 'maplibre-gl';
   const protocol = new pmtiles.Protocol();
   maplibregl.addProtocol('pmtiles', protocol.tile);
   ```

2. **Source definition** – Prefer `url:`.  
   ```json
   "myData": {
     "type": "vector",
     "url": "pmtiles://https://my-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/region.pmtiles"
   }
   ```

3. **CORS & Range support** – Verify the host returns:  
   * `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (or your domain)  
   * `Accept-Ranges: bytes`  
   * `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000` (optional but recommended)

4. **Zoom range** – If you must use `tiles:` add `minzoom`/`maxzoom` that match the archive (run `pmtiles show <file> --metadata` to see them).

5. **Test** – Open the Network tab, reload the page, and confirm the **first request** is a normal GET of the `.pmtiles` file (not a tile request). Then zoom in/out and watch the range requests; they should all be `206 Partial Content` with a non-empty body.

---

## Example: Full minimal style with a PMTiles vector source

```json
{
  "version": 8,
  "sources": {
    "world": {
      "type": "vector",
      "url": "pmtiles://https://example.com/world.pmtiles"
    }
  },
  "layers": [
    {
      "id": "water",
      "type": "fill",
      "source": "world",
      "source-layer": "water",
      "paint": { "fill-color": "#a0c8f0" }
    },
    {
      "id": "roads",
      "type": "line",
      "source": "world",
      "source-layer": "road",
      "paint": { "line-color": "#777", "line-width": 1 }
    }
  ]
}
```

If you really need a template for some reason (e.g., you want to split the data into multiple PMTiles files per region), keep the `url:` for each file and add a **filter** on the source or use **multiple sources** with `bounds` to let MapLibre pick the right one.

---

### TL;DR Recap

* **`tiles:` + template → MapLibre ignores the PMTiles header → assumes `maxzoom: 22`.**  
* When you zoom past the archive’s real maxzoom, the protocol returns empty tiles → blanks.  
* **Fix:** Use `url:` (the PMTiles protocol’s preferred way) or manually set `maxzoom` to the archive’s value.  

That’s why your file looks fine with `pmtiles show` but goes blank on the map. Switch to `url:` (or add the correct `maxzoom`) and the blanks disappear. Happy mapping!
